title: Generate and display the demo-versus-live parity report with staleness flags
body:
## Context
US-PAPER-008 (Should) gives the owner a report of known demo-versus-live differences so expectations are calibrated, and it is the artefact that makes R4 'a gating exercise rather than a re-architecture' (roadmap section 7.1 goal 5). Its NFR forbids the easy implementation: 'the report is generated from a maintained data file plus runtime observations, never hand-written prose only'.

Three behaviours define it: list the known differences with their source and last-verified date; capture operations that fail only in demo as **candidate** parity items; and flag items unverified for 90 days as needing re-verification. The report lives in SCR-137 (Admin: security centre) and is linked from SCR-074.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Backend: load `packages/backend/cv/paper/parity_items.yaml` (seeded by E38-K01) at startup, validate it against a schema (id, area, description, source, severity, last_verified, capability_ref), and expose it via a new `GET /admin/parity` endpoint (add to `docs/plan/22-api-openapi.yaml`, `x-rbac` permission `audit:read`, scope none).
- **Runtime observation capture**: every `CapabilityUnsupported` refusal (E38-T01) and every demo-only exchange error observed by the adapter is recorded as a *candidate* parity item with its operation, error signature, first-seen and last-seen timestamps and an occurrence count - deduplicated by signature, never auto-promoted into the confirmed list.
- **Staleness**: any confirmed item whose `last_verified` is older than 90 days is returned flagged `needs_reverification`; a scheduled job recomputes the flag daily and raises a notification when an item crosses the threshold.
- Re-verification action: an owner-only endpoint marking an item verified (updating `last_verified` and writing an audit row), intended to be driven by re-running the E38-K01 probe harness.
- Frontend on **SCR-137**: the parity table (difference, area, source, last verified, status), the needs-re-verification treatment using text plus icon, the candidate-items inbox with promote/dismiss actions, and empty/loading/error/RBAC-denied states. Components CMP-028, CMP-036, CMP-050, CMP-087, CMP-093, CMP-175, CMP-178.
- A link from SCR-074 to the report, so a user hitting a demo limitation can read why.
- Deep-link support: a `CapabilityUnsupported` refusal carries `parity_item_id`, and the UI links the refusal message to that row.

## Out of scope
- The probe harness that produces verification evidence (E38-K01 built it; this story only records the outcome).
- The paper-fidelity divergence panel (E38-T03 produces the data; its display reuses this screen's patterns but is a separate concern).
- Auto-promoting candidates to confirmed items - deliberately a human decision.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: The report lists known differences with source and date
  Given the seeded parity data file
  When the report is requested
  Then each known difference is listed with its description, source and last-verified date, including no-WS-order-entry-in-demo, batch-order category limits and fee differences

Scenario: A demo-only failure becomes a candidate item
  Given an operation fails only in demo
  When the failure is observed at runtime
  Then it is recorded as a candidate parity item with its error signature and occurrence count, and is not silently merged into the confirmed list

Scenario: Stale items are flagged
  Given an item last verified 91 days ago
  When the report is generated
  Then that item is flagged as needing re-verification and a notification is raised once, not on every generation

Scenario: The report is generated, not authored
  Given the parity data file is modified
  When the report is requested
  Then the output reflects the file without any code change, and a test asserts no report content is hardcoded in the UI

Scenario: An invalid data file fails loudly at startup
  Given a parity item missing a required field
  When the application starts
  Then startup fails with a precise validation error rather than serving a silently incomplete report

Scenario: A refusal links to its parity item
  Given a capability refusal carrying a parity item id
  When the user follows the link
  Then the parity report opens focused on that row

Scenario: Re-verification is audited
  Given the owner marks an item verified
  When the change is saved
  Then last_verified updates and an audit row records who verified it and when
```

## Technical notes / design
- The data file is the source of truth and is version-controlled; the DB holds only runtime observations and verification timestamps, joined at read time. This keeps the curated knowledge reviewable in PRs while the observed knowledge accumulates at runtime.
- Candidate deduplication key: (operation, retCode, normalised retMsg) - normalise out ids and timestamps so one real difference is not recorded as thousands of candidates.
- The staleness notification uses the existing notification/alert delivery path rather than a bespoke mechanism.
- `capability_ref` cross-links each item to an `EnvironmentCapabilities` field, and a test asserts every hard capability restriction has a parity item and vice versa - this is what prevents the code and the report drifting apart.
- The UI renders whatever the API returns, including item types it does not know about, so adding a parity item never requires a frontend release.

## Test plan
- Unit: schema validation of the data file, incl. the startup-failure case.
- Unit: staleness computation at the 89/90/91-day boundaries.
- Unit: candidate deduplication and occurrence counting under repeated identical failures.
- Unit: capability-to-parity-item bidirectional coverage test.
- Contract: `GET /admin/parity` and the verification endpoint against OpenAPI; RBAC denial for non-`audit:read` callers.
- Integration: trigger a capability refusal through the adapter and assert a candidate item appears with the right signature.
- axe-core on the SCR-137 parity section incl. the flagged state.
- E2E (feeds E38-Q02): open the report, follow a deep link from a refusal, mark an item verified and observe the audit row.
- Coverage: >=85% backend, >=80% frontend.

## Security notes
- SCR-137 is the security centre: the report must contain no key material, no account identifiers beyond what the caller may already see, and no raw exchange responses that might embed credentials - candidate items store a normalised signature, not the raw payload.
- Access requires `audit:read`; verification requires owner-level permission and is audited.
- Threat: a stale or wrong parity report giving false confidence before R4 live enablement - mitigated by the staleness flag and the capability cross-link test.
- Data classification: operational/security metadata, internal.

## Accessibility notes
- Real table semantics with header associations; needs-re-verification and candidate states use text plus icon, never colour alone.
- The candidate inbox's promote/dismiss actions have accessible names naming the item.
- Deep-linked rows receive focus and are announced on arrival.
- Empty state explains what would populate the table rather than showing a bare 'no data'.

## Performance notes
- Tens of rows: no virtualisation needed. The report is assembled from an in-memory data file plus one indexed query; target <150 ms p95 (budget #13 read endpoints).
- Candidate recording must be fire-and-forget on the refusal path so it cannot add latency to an order rejection.

## Observability
- Metric `cv_parity_items{status}` gauge (confirmed, candidate, stale).
- Audit `parity.item_verified`, `parity.candidate_promoted`, `parity.candidate_dismissed`.
- Notification when an item becomes stale, delivered once per transition.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Acceptance criteria demonstrated by automated tests referencing each scenario by name.

- [ ] Docs updated: `docs/plan/22-api-openapi.yaml`, `docs/plan/23-ws-protocol.md`, `docs/plan/24-internal-schemas.md`, `docs/plan/21-database-schema.md` reflect shipped behaviour where they diverged.

- [ ] Design sign-off: built screen compared against the Figma spec by a designer (`design-qa`); discrepancies fixed or filed as Bug with priority.
- [ ] a11y: axe-core CI green on the touched screens, manual screen-reader pass recorded, keyboard-only path verified (`docs/plan/05-accessibility-standard.md`).
- [ ] Storybook stories added/updated for every touched component with all states.

## Dependencies

## Branch

title: Reconcile plan docs and ADRs with the shipped paper and parity behaviour
body:
## Context
`docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` section 2.2 requires that the plan docs reflect final shipped behaviour, not the original proposal, wherever they diverged. E38 touches unusually normative documents - `docs/plan/24-internal-schemas.md` section 12 specifies the matcher field by field - so divergence between doc and code here is more damaging than usual: E44 and E43 will read these documents as truth when gating live enablement.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Reconcile `docs/plan/24-internal-schemas.md` section 12 (paper matcher) with the shipped `FillModelConfig`, queue model, fee, funding and margin implementations; correct any default, formula or behaviour that changed during implementation, and mark anything deliberately not implemented in R3 as such.
- Reconcile `docs/plan/20-architecture.md` section 3.7 (Paper Matcher components) and the C11 row with the shipped module layout.
- Ensure `docs/plan/22-api-openapi.yaml` contains the endpoints added by this epic (`POST /exchange-accounts/{accountId}/paper-reset`, `GET /admin/parity`, the parity verification endpoint, `GET /admin/paper-fidelity`) with correct `x-rbac` and `x-idempotency` annotations, and that the contract tests pass.
- Ensure `docs/plan/21-database-schema.md` reflects the `user_account_access` eligibility columns and any paper-ledger/parity-observation tables added, including the migration ids.
- Update `docs/plan/14-screens-catalogue.md` and `docs/plan/15-component-catalogue.md` where the shipped SCR-074/075/079/099/122/137 and CMP-074/075/139 behaviour differs from the written entry.
- Amend `docs/plan/27-adrs/ADR-0026-demo-live-parity.md` with any decision made during implementation, and file a new ADR if a genuinely new architectural decision was taken.
- Add the E38 changelog fragments and confirm `docs/plan/32-risk-register.md` reflects R12's current status given the divergence job's first results.

## Out of scope
- Rewriting documents that did not diverge - this is reconciliation, not a documentation project.
- Producing user-facing help documentation.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Normative sections match the code
  Given docs/plan/24-internal-schemas.md section 12
  When compared field by field against the shipped FillModelConfig and matcher behaviour
  Then every divergence is either corrected in the doc or justified inline as a deliberate deviation

Scenario: New endpoints are in the contract
  Given the endpoints added by this epic
  When the contract tests run
  Then each is present in the OpenAPI document with correct RBAC and idempotency annotations, and the tests pass

Scenario: Screens and components reflect what shipped
  Given the E38 screens and components
  When their catalogue entries are reviewed against the build
  Then any behavioural difference is reflected in the entry

Scenario: Decisions are recorded as ADRs
  Given any architectural decision taken during E38 implementation
  When this ticket completes
  Then it is recorded in an ADR rather than living only in a pull-request discussion
```

## Technical notes / design
- Do this as one pass at the end of the epic rather than piecemeal, so the reviewer sees the whole picture; but file it as a blocking item for the epic's Done so it cannot be quietly skipped.
- Where code and doc disagree and the code is right, change the doc; where the doc is right, file a Bug against the code rather than weakening the doc to match.

## Test plan
- Contract tests (`make contracts`: `openapi_structural`, `ref_closure`, `rbac_coverage`, `error_registry_single_source`, `enum_parity_environment`) must pass after the changes.
- A reviewer independently spot-checks three reconciled claims against the code.

## Security notes
- The security program references (SR-040a in particular) must still accurately describe the implemented control; a doc that overstates a control is a security problem because later work will rely on it.

## Accessibility notes
N/A - documentation.

## Performance notes
- Record the measured numbers from E38-Q03 into the performance standard's tracking section so budgets are backed by observed values rather than estimates.

## Observability
- Ensure the metrics and audit events E38 added are listed in the observability documentation, so operators know what exists.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] All listed documents reviewed and reconciled, with a summary of changes on the ticket.
- [ ] `make contracts` green.
- [ ] ADR-0016 amended or a new ADR filed for any implementation-time decision.
- [ ] Changelog fragments present.
- [ ] Reviewed by the Architect.
- [ ] `docs/plan/32-risk-register.md` updated with R12's status given the first divergence results.

## Dependencies
- `blocked_by: E38-S03`, `E38-S08`, `E38-T03` - the implementations whose final behaviour is being documented.

## Branch
`chore/e38-doc-reconcile`; PR size: docs-only.

## References
- `docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` section 2.2
- `docs/plan/24-internal-schemas.md` section 12, section 19 contract tests

title: Abuse cases, permission checks and SAST rules for the environment boundary
body:
## Context
E38-X01 enumerated the threats; this ticket attacks the built system and turns the durable findings into automated rules. `docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` section 8 requires a manual abuse-case check for anything touching RBAC, and the R3 quality gate requires a targeted abuse-case review of privilege escalation before the train closes.

The specific claims under attack are the ones the epic's safety rests on: that no demo session can reach live, that no simulated order can reach the exchange, and that no manager can grant themselves live access.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Execute the abuse-case list from E38-X01 against the staging build, at minimum:
  1. Craft a live-targeting request from a demo session via every trading route (driven from the route list in E38-T02), including direct API calls bypassing the UI entirely.
  2. Attempt to switch to live without step-up, with an expired elevation, with the `live_trading` flag off, and by replaying a previously successful switch request.
  3. Attempt to act on a live grant before acknowledgement.
  4. Attempt self-granting of live eligibility as a manager, and via a crafted `PUT /users/{userId}/account-access` payload targeting one's own user id.
  5. Attempt to create and to submit a mixed-environment trade group.
  6. Attempt to make the paper matcher perform a network call (dependency injection, config override, monkeypatch-style manipulation of the adapter routing).
  7. Attempt to reset a live account's balance via the paper-reset endpoint.
  8. Attempt to read another user's grants through the not-permitted message, the parity report or an error body.
  9. Attempt to flood candidate parity items to exhaust storage.
- Verify for each: refusal, no state change, an audit row of the right severity, and no information leaked in the response.
- Commit durable detections: Semgrep rules forbidding (a) a Bybit hostname outside `capabilities.py`, (b) a trading route handler without the environment dependency, (c) an HTTP/WS client import inside `cv/paper/`; plus a ZAP/DAST profile exercising the cross-environment routes.
- Run SCA and secrets scanning over the new code paths and triage findings.

## Out of scope
- The threat model itself (E38-X01) and the final review (E38-X03).
- Pen-testing (E43, an R4 activity) - this is internal abuse-case testing, deliberately narrower.
- Load-based denial of service beyond the candidate-item flood case (E38-Q03 covers capacity).

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every abuse case is executed and recorded
  Given the abuse-case list from the threat model
  When testing completes
  Then each case has a recorded outcome with evidence, and any success is filed as a priority p0 security defect

Scenario: Cross-environment attempts are refused on every route
  Given the full trading route list
  When a live-targeting request is crafted from a demo session on each
  Then every route refuses with 403, changes no state, and writes a high-severity audit row

Scenario: The simulator cannot be made to reach the network
  Given attempts to route the paper matcher through a real transport
  When each is tried
  Then none succeeds, and the structural Semgrep rule prevents the import that would enable it

Scenario: Self-granting is impossible
  Given a manager account
  When eligibility self-grant is attempted directly against the API
  Then it is refused and audited, and the attempt does not partially apply

Scenario: Durable rules are committed and run in CI
  When this ticket completes
  Then the three Semgrep rules and the ZAP profile are committed and executing in CI, failing the build on violation

Scenario: A replayed switch request does not re-switch
  Given a captured successful switch request
  When it is replayed after the elevation expires
  Then it is refused rather than honoured
```

## Technical notes / design
- Testing is black-box against staging plus white-box review of the isolation middleware, the adapter routing and the eligibility derivation - the combination matters because a route can pass black-box testing while having the guard attached in a way a refactor would silently drop.
- The route-list-driven approach means this test automatically covers routes added after E38-T02 was written, as long as the OpenAPI document is the source.
- Semgrep rules are written to fail on the *pattern*, not on a filename allowlist, so moving a file does not defeat them.
- Evidence for each case: request, response, database state before and after, and the audit row (or its absence, which is itself a finding).

## Test plan
- The abuse cases are the test artefact. Each durable rule must be demonstrated to fire against a deliberately introduced violation before it is accepted.
- Findings are re-verified after fixes within this ticket.

## Security notes
- This ticket *is* the security testing: SAST (Semgrep/Bandit/CodeQL), DAST (ZAP), SCA (pip-audit/npm audit) and secrets scanning over E38's code, plus manual abuse-case execution per `docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` section 8.
- Any successful abuse case is a `priority/p0-critical` defect that blocks the R3 gate, not a backlog item.

## Accessibility notes
N/A - security testing. One cross-check: confirm that refusal messages remain accessible (associated with their control, announced) while not disclosing more than they should.

## Performance notes
- The candidate-parity-item flood case is also a capacity check: confirm deduplication bounds growth, so a repeating demo error cannot fill the disk.

## Observability
- Verify every refusal produces the audit event and metric the threat model specified, at the right severity; a missing audit row on a refused abuse attempt is itself a finding.

- [ ] Findings recorded in the epic's STRIDE worksheet under `docs/security/threat-models/E38-paper-trading.md`.
- [ ] Every Critical/High finding fixed or accepted-risk with Owner sign-off recorded (`docs/plan/04-security-program.md`).
- [ ] SAST (Semgrep/Bandit/CodeQL), SCA (pip-audit/npm audit) and secrets scan clean or triaged on the touched paths.
- [ ] Security engineer review comment present on the ticket.
- [ ] Any new detection rule committed to the Semgrep/ZAP rule set and running in CI.
- [ ] `docs/plan/32-risk-register.md` updated if the review surfaced or retired a risk.

## Dependencies
- `blocked_by: E38-X01` (the case list), `E38-T02`, `E38-S02`, `E38-S03`, `E38-S07` (the controls under attack must exist).

## Branch
`test/e38-abuse-cases`; PR size: rules plus DAST profile plus findings doc.

body:
## Context
`docs/plan/30-release-roadmap.md` section 7.4 requires all Critical and High STRIDE findings closed before the R3 train ends, and E44 (live enablement) depends on E38 - the roadmap dependency graph has `E38 --> E44`. Whatever E38 leaves unresolved becomes a live-money problem in R4.

This is the closing gate: confirm every control the threat model asked for exists, works, and is verified by a test that will keep running.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Verify each control from `docs/security/threat-models/E38-paper-trading.md` is implemented, with its verifying test present and passing: the capability matrix, the isolation middleware and its route-coverage gate, the switch's step-up and flag gates, eligibility enforcement and the acknowledgement gate, the paper matcher's structural no-transport guarantee, the reset's env refusal, and the parity report's non-disclosure of raw payloads.
- Confirm every finding from E38-X02 is fixed or has a written Owner-accepted risk with an expiry date.
- Confirm SAST, DAST, SCA and secrets scanning are clean or triaged on all E38 paths, and that the three Semgrep rules plus the ZAP profile are running as required checks.
- Confirm audit coverage: every action the threat model marked as needing non-repudiation writes an audit row of the specified severity, verified by executing each action and inspecting the log.
- Produce the **E38 input to the R4 live-enablement gate**: a written statement of what E38 guarantees about environment separation, what it explicitly does not guarantee, and which assumptions E44 must re-verify before the flag is turned on.
- Post the Security engineer sign-off comment required by `docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md`, and update `docs/plan/32-risk-register.md`.

## Out of scope
- New security testing (E38-X02 did that).
- The R4 pen-test (E43) and the live-enablement gate itself (E44) - this produces input to them.
- Other epics' sign-offs.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every control is verified present and effective
  Given the threat model's control list
  When the review completes
  Then each control is confirmed implemented with a named passing test, or is recorded as an accepted risk with Owner sign-off and an expiry date

Scenario: No Critical or High finding remains open
  Given the findings from E38-X02 and E38-Q06
  When sign-off is considered
  Then no Critical or High finding is open, and the epic cannot be marked Done while one is

Scenario: Durable gates are actually required checks
  Given the Semgrep rules, the route-coverage test and the ZAP profile
  When the branch protection configuration is inspected
  Then each is a required check, so a future PR cannot merge past them

Scenario: Audit coverage is verified by execution
  Given each action requiring non-repudiation
  When it is performed on staging
  Then the corresponding audit row exists at the specified severity, verified by inspection rather than by reading the code

Scenario: The R4 handover statement exists
  When this ticket completes
  Then a written statement of E38's guarantees, non-guarantees and the assumptions E44 must re-verify is committed and linked from the E44 epic
```

## Technical notes / design
- The review is evidence-based: for each control, the reviewer records the test name and the CI run in which it passed, not merely a code reference, because a test that exists but does not run is not a control.
- The 'non-guarantees' section of the R4 statement is the most valuable output: it should name explicitly, for example, that E38 proves separation under tested conditions on demo and that live behaviour is re-verified by E44 and E43's pen-test.
- Cross-check the structural-versus-enforced control classification from E38-X01: structural controls should have a compile-time or import-time test, enforced controls a runtime test.

## Test plan
- No new testing; verification of existing test evidence. Any control found without a verifying test causes a Task to be filed and blocks sign-off until it exists.

## Security notes
- This ticket *is* the sign-off gate required by `docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` section 2.2 and section 8, and by the R3 quality gate.
- It must be performed by the Security engineer, not by the implementing engineers.

## Performance notes
- Confirms that no control was weakened for performance reasons during implementation; any such trade-off must appear as an accepted risk rather than as an undocumented change.

## Observability
- Confirms the security-relevant metrics and alerts exist and are wired to a destination: capability refusals, environment rejections, switch failures, refused resets, live-eligibility changes.

- State sweep: every row of the state matrix forced (via the E40-Q01 fixtures) and screenshotted, including delivery-failed, auto-disarmed, vocabulary-unavailable and desktop-permission-denied.

Scenario: Every state was actually seen (edge)

Delivery is executed by parallel AI agents with a single human owner (`@basiltt`). Where this ticket's text assumes the original 15-person org, apply these substitutions — they are binding and satisfy the corresponding DoR/DoD items:
- **Architect / CDO / Security-engineer sign-off or countersignature** → the **owner's** `approved` comment on this issue, or owner merge of the PR. No other human role exists. Do not block on a missing countersignature — proceed and record "owner approval pending" in the PR.
- **Design tooling**: *Figma* → **Penpot** (`docs/design/README.md`); frames on a page named after this ticket; exports via `docs/design/_tools/penpot_export.py`. Bind only to semantic tokens in `packages/ui/tokens/`.
- **Moderated usability / participant sessions** → a documented **heuristic evaluation** (Nielsen + the trading-specific heuristics in `docs/plan/05-accessibility-standard.md`), a written session protocol ready for the owner to run later, and an **owner walkthrough** checklist posted on the issue. Never fabricate participants, timings or quotes; label all findings `(heuristic)`.
- **CVD / contrast validation** → computed programmatically (WCAG contrast matrix over the token JSON; CVD simulation via a documented script), attached as artefacts.
- **Spikes**: findings go to `docs/plan/spikes/<KEY>.md` via a normal PR (branch `spike/<epic>-<slug>`); any ADR named by the spike uses the **next free number** in `docs/plan/27-adrs/` (ADR-0001…0016 are taken).
- **Dependencies**: `blocked_by` now lists the concrete prerequisite tickets (not whole epics). Start when those are **merged** (In Test or Done).
- Anything that genuinely needs a human that is not the owner (external pen-test vendor, legal) stays as-is and is flagged `needs-owner` on the issue.

title: Write the alert test plan and automate the E2E and contract suites
body:
## Context
Merged from the former E40-Q01 and E40-Q01: the black-box plan and the automation that implements it are one QA slice.

### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
`docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md` requires a black-box test plan per feature, written from the specification rather than from the code. Alerts are unusually testable on paper — every trigger mode, gate and channel has a stated behaviour — and unusually easy to get wrong in ways unit tests miss (a cooldown consumed by a snoozed alert, a storm summary that loses a firing, a mute that silences a risk event). This ticket writes the oracle before the implementation is finished.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
R3's E2E gate (`docs/plan/30-release-roadmap.md` §7.4) explicitly names "alert firing" as required Playwright coverage on web *and* Electron. This ticket turns E40-Q01's plan into the automated suites that make the gate real.

## Scope / Deliverables
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
- `docs/qa/test-plans/e40-alerts.md` — a black-box plan covering:
  - **Trigger-mode matrix**: `once` / `every_time` / `once_per_bar` × condition-true-once / true-continuously / true-across-a-bar-boundary / true-on-a-revised-bar, with the expected firing count per cell.
  - **Gating matrix**: enabled, deleted, expired, snoozed, muted symbol, muted category, quiet hours, cooldown, storm limit — including the ordering assertion that a snoozed alert does **not** consume its cooldown.
  - **Critical-override matrix**: every entry of the E40-D01 ratified list × every mute/quiet-hours combination, asserting delivery in all cells. This is the test coverage the US-ALRT-006 NFR demands.
  - **Channel matrix**: in-app / desktop (granted, denied, unsupported) / email (success, transient failure, permanent failure) / webhook (flag off in R3) / push (rejected), asserting in every case that the in-app record exists and is unaffected.
  - **Condition-family coverage**: price (US-ALRT-001), indicator/metric (US-ALRT-002), order-flow and detector (US-ALRT-003) — at least one authored alert per family, each with the expected firing against a named recorded window.
  - **History and export**: firing history completeness incl. suppressed entries, 90-day retention expectation, CSV export content.
  - **RBAC/scoping**: own-alerts-only for read, write, ack and delivery listing.
- **Fixtures**: named recorded Bybit windows (from E16/E26) that deterministically produce — (a) a single clean price cross, (b) an RSI bar-close cross, (c) a stacked-imbalance burst suitable for storm testing, (d) a metric-source-loss event for the auto-disarm case. Each fixture documented with symbol, window, expected events and expected firing count.
- **Fault-injection helpers** (shared with E40-D03 and E40-Q02): force delivery-failed, force desktop-permission-denied, force vocabulary-unavailable, force a 412 concurrent edit, force a storm.
- **Exploratory charters** (session-based, 60–90 min each): "author the strangest alert you can and try to make it act"; "make the notification centre lie about the unread count"; "configure yourself into silence and see what still reaches you"; "fire a storm and try to lose a firing"; "break the alert editor with the keyboard only".
- Traceability table mapping every US-ALRT scenario to at least one test case id.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
- **Playwright E2E (web + Electron)**, driven against staging (demo) with the E26 replay harness supplying the recorded windows:
  1. *Author and fire a price alert* — create via SCR-091 → appears Active in SCR-090 → replay the window → toast appears with the triggering value → detail drawer shows the metric snapshot → item in SCR-014 → ack → badge clears.
  2. *Indicator alert on bar close* — RSI(14) 15m crosses below 30; assert it fires on bar close and not intrabar, and that the editor stated which.
  3. *Order-flow alert* — stacked imbalance depth ≥3; assert the firing carries the price range, direction and the "(estimated)" qualifier.
  4. *One-shot vs recurring* — one-shot disarms after firing; recurring re-arms after cooldown.
  5. *Snooze and mute* — snooze moves the alert to the Snoozed tab with remaining time; muting ETHUSDT silences sound/desktop while the record persists.
  6. *Critical override* — with everything muted and quiet hours on, a risk notification still delivers (driven by an E39 risk event injected via the fixture).
  7. *Storm* — 25 firings in a minute produce a summary plus individually-recorded suppressed entries, all visible in history.
  8. *Delivery failure* — desktop permission denied shows the blocked chip and remediation; the in-app record is unaffected.
  9. *Bulk actions with a partial failure* — result reported per item.
  10. *Electron-specific* — an OS notification is raised while the window is unfocused and clicking it focuses the window at the right detail.
- **Contract suites**: every `/alerts*` and `/notifications` operation and response code validated against `22-api-openapi.yaml`; the `alerts` WS payload validated against `23-ws-protocol.md` §15.7, including `unacked_count` and the `unacked_only` option; a schema-drift test that fails when implementation and document diverge.
- **Integration suite**: fixture replay → expected firing sequence, run in CI on every push to alert modules; determinism asserted by running the critical fixture twice in one job and diffing the sequences.
- CI wiring: the alert E2E suite runs in the nightly full pass and as a required check on alert-touching PRs; flake budget and quarantine policy per `docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md`.

## Out of scope
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
Writing the automation (E40-Q01). Performance/chaos scripts (E40-Q02). A11y audit (E40-Q02). Security abuse cases (E40-X01) — though the plan cross-references them.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
Perf/load/chaos (E40-Q02). A11y audit (E40-Q02). Security abuse cases (E40-X01). The webhook path (E40-S03, R5).

## Acceptance criteria
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
```gherkin
Scenario: Every Must scenario has a test case
  When the traceability table is checked against 11-user-stories.md section 24
  Then every Gherkin scenario in US-ALRT-001 through US-ALRT-006 maps to at least one numbered test case
Scenario: Fixtures are deterministic
  Given each named recorded window
  When it is replayed three times
  Then the expected firing count and sequence are identical every time
Scenario: The critical-override matrix is exhaustive (edge)
  Then every entry of the ratified override list appears in the matrix against every mute and quiet-hours combination, with no cell left unspecified
Scenario: A cell with no defined behaviour is escalated, not invented (failure)
  Given a matrix cell whose expected result the specification does not state
  Then a question is raised on the owning ticket and the cell is marked blocked until answered, rather than the tester guessing
```
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
```gherkin
Scenario: The suite covers every Must story end to end
  When the suite runs
  Then at least one scenario exercises each of US-ALRT-001 through US-ALRT-006 against a real replayed window
Scenario: Contract drift fails the build
  Given the implementation changes a response field without updating the OpenAPI document
  Then the contract test fails with a message naming the field
Scenario: The suite is deterministic (edge)
  When the critical fixture runs twice in one CI job
  Then the firing sequences are byte-identical and the suite passes both times
Scenario: A flaky test is quarantined, not deleted (failure)
  Given a test fails intermittently
  Then it is quarantined with a filed Bug and a named owner rather than removed or retried into silence
```

## Technical notes / design
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
Fixtures are recorded windows, not synthetic streams, so the tests exercise the real ingestion path. Register each fixture in the shared fixture catalogue with a checksum so a silently changed recording fails loudly.

The fault-injection helpers are shipped as a test-only API surface guarded by an environment flag that is impossible to enable in production builds — a unit test asserts the guard.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
Drive time deterministically: the replay harness controls the clock, so cooldown and quiet-hours scenarios do not depend on wall-clock sleeps. Where a real elapsed period is unavoidable, use the fault-injection helper to advance the server's notion of time rather than sleeping.

Electron coverage runs against the packaged shell so the IPC notification path is genuinely exercised, not mocked.

Assert on server state as well as UI state (delivery rows, statuses, audit rows) — a UI that looks right over a broken record is exactly the failure mode alerts have.

## Test plan
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
This ticket *is* a test plan; its own verification is the review by the QA lead, the epic owner and one backend engineer, plus the check that E40-Q01 can automate directly from it without re-deriving expectations.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
Self-verifying: the suite is the deliverable. Validate it by mutation — disable the cooldown gate, the storm suppressor and the critical-override check in turn, and confirm a specific test fails for each. That mutation check runs once at merge and is documented in the PR.

## Security notes
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
Fixtures may embed real recorded market data but must contain no account identifiers, keys or balances; scrub and verify before checking in. The fault-injection surface is itself a threat if it reaches production — hence the guard and its test.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
The suite runs against staging (demo) only, never live. Test accounts use demo keys with withdrawal off. No real key material enters a fixture or a CI log; a secrets-scan runs over the suite's artifacts.

## Accessibility notes
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
The plan includes the keyboard-only exploratory charter; the formal audit is E40-Q02.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
The E2E suite includes axe-core scans on `/alerts`, the editor modal, the notification drawer and the settings matrix as smoke-level gates; the deep audit is E40-Q02.

## Performance notes
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
The plan states the budgets under test so functional testers notice a breach: ≤1 s to record, ≤2 s to toast, ≤1 Hz list updates, 250 ms WS cadence.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
Suite wall-clock ≤12 min in CI; the replay harness runs at accelerated time so a 60 s storm window does not cost 60 s.

## Observability
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
Test cases assert the metrics and audit events are emitted, not merely the UI outcome — a firing that produces no `cv_alert_fires_total` increment is a defect.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
Test runs publish the standard JUnit + trace artifacts; failures attach the Playwright trace and the server's alert metrics snapshot so a failure is diagnosable without a re-run.

## Definition of Done
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
- [ ] Test plan merged with the traceability table complete.
- [ ] Four fixtures registered, checksummed and proven deterministic over three runs.
- [ ] Fault-injection helpers merged with their production guard and test.
- [ ] Five exploratory charters written.
- [ ] Reviewed by QA lead, epic owner and a backend engineer.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
- [ ] Ten E2E scenarios green on web and, where applicable, Electron.
- [ ] Contract and WS-schema suites green and wired as required checks.
- [ ] Determinism assertion in CI.
- [ ] Mutation check documented in the PR.
- [ ] Suite runtime within budget; flake policy applied.
- [ ] QA lead review; PR merged via merge queue.

## Dependencies
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
`E40-D02` (states and copy to test against), `E40-D01` (ratified critical-override list, the oracle for that matrix), `E16`/`E26` for recorded windows.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
`E40-Q01` (plan and fixtures), `E40-S01`/`S02`/`S03` (the surfaces under test), `E26` replay harness, `E39` for the risk-event injection.

## Branch
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
`test/e40-alerts-plan`.
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
`test/e40-alerts-e2e`.

## References
### Part A — Black-box test plan, fixtures and exploratory charters
- `docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md`
- `docs/plan/04-security-program.md`
- `docs/plan/05-accessibility-standard.md`
- `docs/plan/06-performance-and-load-standard.md`
- `docs/plan/11-user-stories.md` §24 ALRT
- `docs/plan/14-screens-catalogue.md` SCR-014, SCR-090, SCR-091, SCR-092, SCR-115
- `docs/plan/22-api-openapi.yaml` `/alerts*`, `/notifications`
- `docs/plan/23-ws-protocol.md` §15.7 `AlertUpdate`
- `docs/plan/30-release-roadmap.md` §7.4 quality gates
### Part B — E2E and contract automation for alert authoring, firing and delivery
- `docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md`
- `docs/plan/04-security-program.md`
- `docs/plan/05-accessibility-standard.md`

- `docs/plan/14-screens-catalogue.md` SCR-014, SCR-090, SCR-091, SCR-092, SCR-115
- `docs/plan/22-api-openapi.yaml` `/alerts*`, `/notifications`
- `docs/plan/23-ws-protocol.md` §15.7 `AlertUpdate`
- `docs/plan/30-release-roadmap.md` §7.4 quality gates

## Agent execution brief

**Read first**
1. docs/plan/28-statechart-catalogue.md (alert evaluator machine, E40-T03)

title: Run alert perf/storm/chaos and a11y audits, then give QA sign-off
body:
## Context
Merged from the former E40-Q02, E40-Q02 and E40-Q02 — the non-functional verification passes and the QA sign-off that consumes them.

### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
Alerts have hard latency budgets (≤1 s to record, ≤2 s to toast) and a failure mode — losing or duplicating a notification across a crash — that only chaos testing surfaces. R3's quality gates require load and chaos coverage; this ticket supplies both for E40 and produces the numbers E40-T05 records as the baseline.
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
E40-D01 wrote the a11y contract in Figma; this ticket verifies the built product against it. Notifications are where WCAG 2.2.1 (no timing loss) and 4.1.3 (status messages) are most commonly failed, and R3's a11y gate requires a verified pass before the train closes.
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
Epic DoD requires an epic-level QA pass, not just per-child sign-offs. This ticket runs the unscripted testing that finds what the matrices did not, curates what E40 contributes to the permanent regression pack, and records the sign-off that lets the epic close.

## Scope / Deliverables
### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
- **Load profile (k6 + a backend harness)**, reusing the benchmark harness from E40-K01:
  - 500 armed alerts across 20 symbols under a recorded high-rate window; assert p95 condition-met → `alert_deliveries` committed ≤1 s and p99 ≤2 s;
  - 50 concurrent WS subscribers on the `alerts` topic; assert the 250 ms cadence holds and no subscriber receives a truncated or out-of-order delta;
  - `GET /notifications` at page size 500 against ≥1M rows across the four source tables; assert p95 <200 ms;
  - subscription-sharing assertion: 500 alerts over 40 distinct conditions must create 40 metric subscriptions, not 500.
- **Storm scenario**: drive the stacked-imbalance fixture until the suppressor engages; assert the summary is produced, every individual firing is still recorded, the UI stays responsive (frontend frame budget measured), and `cv_alert_suppressed_total{reason="storm"}` matches the arithmetic exactly.
- **Chaos scenarios** (per `docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md`):
  1. **Kill mid-fire** — SIGKILL the API between the delivery insert and the outbox poller run; on restart assert exactly-once delivery and no lost firing.
  2. **Postgres failover during a firing burst** — assert no duplicate deliveries and no lost outbox rows.
  3. **WS disconnect during a storm** — client reconnects, receives a correct snapshot with an accurate `unacked_count`, and no delivery is lost or double-counted.
  4. **Metric source loss** — the referenced source goes away mid-window; assert auto-disarm with an explanatory delivery, and correct recovery when the source returns.
  5. **Email relay down** — assert per-channel failure isolation: the in-app record is unaffected and one channel-failure notification is raised, not one per attempt.
  6. **Outbox poller stall** — pause the poller, accumulate depth, resume; assert catch-up without duplicates and that the depth alert fired.
- **Soak**: 24 h with 200 armed alerts on the staging demo feed; assert no memory growth beyond the agreed envelope, no outbox dead rows, and no drift between `fire_count` and the delivery row count.
- Results published to the perf dashboard and recorded against `docs/plan/06-performance-and-load-standard.md`; a regression gate at +5% p95 wired into the nightly run.
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
- Automated: axe-core across `/alerts`, the SCR-091 modal, the SCR-014 drawer, the SCR-092 detail drawer and the SCR-115 settings section, in dark, light and high-contrast themes, at 100% and 200% zoom — wired as a CI gate for those routes.
- Manual screen-reader passes with **NVDA/Firefox** and **VoiceOver/Safari**, plus the Electron shell, covering:
  - a single firing (is the toast announced politely and does focus stay put?);
  - a burst of 25 firings (does announcement throttling produce a summary rather than a flood?);
  - an order rejection arriving during alert chatter (does it reach the separate `role="alert"` region promptly?);
  - the notification drawer opening on a new event (does it avoid stealing focus?);
  - the settings matrix (are row and column headers announced, and is a locked row announced as locked with its reason?).
- **Keyboard-only sweep**: every action in every surface reachable and operable without a mouse — tabs, filters, bulk selection, row actions, snooze menu, editor authoring end to end, mark-all-read, `Shift+click` equivalent, sound preview, quiet-hours fields.
- **Timing audit (WCAG 2.2.1)**: every auto-dismissing toast proven to have a persistent record; pause-on-hover/focus verified; no information exists only transiently.
- **Non-colour encoding** verification for severity, status, snoozed, disabled and delivery-failed.
- Contrast measurement of every state in every theme, including focus rings at ≥3:1.
- `prefers-reduced-motion` verification on toast, stack collapse and drawer.
- Findings logged with WCAG references and severity; blockers/majors fixed inside E40, minors triaged into E47.
- Report at `docs/qa/a11y/e40-alerts-audit.md`.
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
- Execute the five exploratory charters from E40-Q01 as timeboxed session-based tests (60–90 min each), against staging (demo) with the replay harness:
  1. "Author the strangest alert you can and try to make it act" — the invariant hunt.
  2. "Make the notification centre lie about the unread count."
  3. "Configure yourself into silence and see what still reaches you" — the critical-override hunt.
  4. "Fire a storm and try to lose a firing."
  5. "Break the alert editor with the keyboard only."
- Session sheets recorded (charter, duration, areas covered, bugs, questions, follow-up charters spawned) per `docs/plan/03-testing-strategy.md`'s session-based model.
- **Regression pack curation**: select the subset of E40-Q01/Q03 tests that enter the permanent regression suite — at minimum the invariant test (an alert cannot act), the critical-override matrix, exactly-once-under-restart, and the storm-conservation assertion — and wire them into the release regression job.
- Defect triage: every finding filed with `priority/*`, a repro, and the layer that should have caught it (feeding the test-gap analysis); P0/P1 fixed before the epic closes.
- **Epic-level QA sign-off comment** on E40 recording pass/fail per US-ALRT story, the residual risk, and any explicit deviation (e.g. webhook untested because it is flagged off and descoped to R5).
- Contribution to the R3 exit-criteria evidence pack: the alert-firing E2E coverage named in §7.4.

## Out of scope
### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
Functional E2E (E40-Q01), a11y (E40-Q02), security abuse cases (E40-X01). Webhook egress load (E40-S03, R5).
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
Functional testing (E40-Q01). Design fidelity (E40-D03). Non-alert surfaces.
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
Writing new automation (E40-Q01). Fixing defects (the owning ticket does that). Security sign-off (E40-X01).

## Acceptance criteria
### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
```gherkin
Scenario: Latency budgets hold under load
  Given 500 armed alerts across 20 symbols on the recorded high-rate window
  Then p95 condition-to-record is at most 1 s and p99 at most 2 s, recorded in the perf dashboard
Scenario: Exactly-once survives a kill
  Given the API is SIGKILLed between the delivery insert and dispatch
  When it restarts
  Then the pending outbox row is delivered exactly once and no firing is lost
Scenario: A storm never loses a firing (edge)
  Given 25 qualifying firings inside 60 s
  Then the suppressed count plus the delivered count equals 25 exactly, and all 25 are retrievable from history
Scenario: Subscription sharing does not regress (failure)
  Given 500 alerts over 40 distinct conditions
  Then exactly 40 metric subscriptions exist; a higher number fails the run
Scenario: A soak reveals no drift (edge)
  Given the 24 h soak
  Then fire_count equals the delivery-row count for every alert, memory is within envelope, and there are no dead outbox rows
```
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
```gherkin
Scenario: Automated checks are clean
  When axe-core runs across the five surfaces in every theme at 100% and 200% zoom
  Then there are zero serious or critical violations, and the check is wired as a CI gate
Scenario: A burst does not flood the screen reader
  Given 25 alerts fire within a minute with a screen reader active
  Then a summary is announced rather than 25 individual announcements, and the items remain individually readable on demand
Scenario: A critical rejection is not queued behind chatter (edge)
  Given a stream of alert toasts and an order rejection
  Then the rejection is announced through the separate assertive region without waiting for the polite queue to drain
Scenario: Nothing is lost to timing (failure)
  Given any auto-dismissing toast
  Then its content is demonstrably retrievable from the notification centre afterwards
Scenario: A locked preference row is understandable (edge)
  Given the risk-events row in the settings matrix
  Then the screen reader announces it as locked and conveys why, not merely as disabled
```
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
```gherkin
Scenario: All charters are executed and recorded
  Then five session sheets exist, each with its charter, duration, coverage notes and findings
Scenario: The regression pack is wired and green
  Then the selected tests run in the release regression job and pass on the release candidate
Scenario: Every Must story has an explicit verdict
  Then the sign-off comment records pass or fail for US-ALRT-001 through US-ALRT-006 individually, with evidence links
Scenario: A P1 defect blocks sign-off (failure)
  Given an open P0 or P1 defect in E40 scope
  Then QA sign-off is withheld and the epic cannot reach Done
Scenario: Untested scope is declared, not implied (edge)
  Given webhook delivery is flagged off and descoped to R5
  Then the sign-off states it explicitly as untested-by-design with the descoping reference, rather than silently omitting it
```

## Technical notes / design
### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
Chaos uses the existing fault-injection framework (process kill, container pause, Postgres failover via the compose topology) rather than in-code hooks, so the tests exercise real failure rather than a simulation of it.

Exactly-once is asserted from the data, not from logs: count delivery rows per firing and assert the outbox `(topic, dedup_key)` uniqueness held.

The frontend frame-budget measurement during the storm uses the same tracing approach as the chart-engine benchmarks so the numbers are comparable.
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
Test against the built application on staging (demo) with the E40-Q01 fault-injection helpers driving the burst, the rejection and the permission-denied states — the hard-to-reach states are exactly the ones most likely to be inaccessible.

Verify against the E40-D01 contract document clause by clause; a contract clause with no corresponding verification step is itself a finding.
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
Run charters against a realistic data state (a populated alert set, a busy notification history), not an empty install — the interesting defects in a notification system appear at volume.

Spawn follow-up charters when a session finds a rich seam; record them even if they cannot be run within the sprint, so R5 hardening inherits a concrete list.

## Test plan
### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
The scripts are the deliverable. Validate them by mutation: remove the outbox dedup index in a scratch environment and confirm the exactly-once test fails; disable the suppressor and confirm the storm test fails.
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
Automated axe-core plus scripted manual passes with recorded evidence (screen-reader transcripts and short screen recordings attached to the ticket).
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
This ticket executes tests rather than defining them. Its own quality check is the test-gap analysis: for each defect found exploratorily, name the automated layer that should have caught it and file the automation gap.

## Security notes
### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
Load scripts run against staging (demo) with demo credentials only. Generated load must respect the exchange rate-limit governor — a load test that trips Bybit's connection limits is a self-inflicted incident, so connection counts are bounded and documented.
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
Confirm no assistive-technology surface announces content the visual UI redacts — specifically that no webhook URL, secret or account credential is ever in an accessible name, description or live-region announcement.
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
Charter 1 and charter 3 are effectively abuse-case exploration; any security-relevant finding is routed immediately to E40-X01/E40-X01 and to the Security engineer, not merely filed as a Bug.

## Accessibility notes

### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
This ticket is the accessibility verification for the epic; its sign-off is a precondition for the epic's DoD a11y checkbox.

## Performance notes

### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract

### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
Charters run with the perf dashboard open so a subjective "this feels slow" can be attached to a metric rather than a feeling.

## Observability

Runs export `cv_alert_eval_latency_seconds`, `cv_alert_delivery_latency_seconds{channel}`, `cv_alert_suppressed_total`, `cv_outbox_depth`, `cv_alert_subscriptions` to the perf dashboard with the run id, so a regression can be attributed to a commit.
### Part B — Accessibility audit against the a11y contract
N/A.
### Part C — Exploratory charters, regression pack and QA sign-off
Sessions verify that every user-visible event has a corresponding metric or audit record — an observability gap found here is filed as a defect against the owning ticket.

## Definition of Done
### Part A — Performance, load, storm and chaos scenarios
- [ ] Load, storm, six chaos scenarios and the 24 h soak implemented and green.
- [ ] Results recorded against the standard; baseline published.

## Dependencies

title: Threat-model, abuse-test and security sign-off the alert system
body:
## Context
Merged from the former E40-X01, E40-X01 and E40-X01 into one security ticket spanning the threat model, the abuse-case implementation and the final sign-off. The ticket spans S17-S19 and is scheduled in its completion sprint (Sprint 19): Part A is delivered early in Sprint 17 so E40-T02 can implement the notify-only invariant against a written threat model, while Parts B and C run after E40-Q02 on the shipped system.

### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
`docs/plan/04-security-program.md` requires a STRIDE model per epic, and `docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` §2.1 makes the kickoff a DoR item for any epic touching an execution-adjacent surface. Alerts look benign — they only notify — but they sit on the rule IR, they can be configured to make an outbound network call, they render user-authored text into other users' notification surfaces, and muting them is a way to hide an attack. This model is produced **before** implementation so its controls land in E40-T02/T03/T04 rather than being retrofitted.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
E40-X01's findings become code here. The controls that matter are the ones with a test that fails when they regress — particularly the invariant that an alert can never act, which is an assertion about *all possible inputs*, not about the inputs someone happened to think of.
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
`docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` §2.2 requires a Security engineer sign-off before an epic with a `security` label can close, and §7.4 of the roadmap requires the R3 train's security findings to be closed or explicitly accepted. This ticket is the white-box review that pairs with E40-X01's black-box suite.

## Scope / Deliverables
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
- Data-flow diagram of M22: author (SCR-091) → compiler → `alerts` table → evaluator (metric bus) → firing transaction → `alert_deliveries` + `outbox` → dispatcher → channels (in-app WS, Electron desktop, email relay, webhook) → user; plus the read paths (`/alerts`, `/alerts/deliveries`, `/notifications`, WS `alerts`) and the preference path (SCR-115).
- STRIDE analysis per element and per data flow, with at minimum:
  - **S** — forging a delivery (can a client fabricate a notification?); impersonating the Electron shell's permission callback.
  - **T** — tampering with firing history (mitigated by the append-only trigger); last-writer-wins edits (mitigated by `If-Match`); tampering with the critical-override list.
  - **R** — repudiation of "why did this fire" (mitigated by the evaluation snapshot in `alert_deliveries.context` and the audit events).
  - **I** — cross-user alert/delivery disclosure; secrets leaking into a message template, a notification body or a webhook payload; `/notifications` union leaking events the caller lacks permission for; a screen-reader announcement reading redacted content.
  - **D** — alert-count exhaustion; unthrottled detector-driven evaluation; `ack-all` as an unbounded statement; outbox growth; webhook amplification.
  - **E** — the headline one: an alert that can act. Any path by which `condition_ir` reaches an action, directly or through a future rule-IR node kind.
- **Abuse cases** written for E40-X01: smuggle an action node; craft a template that exfiltrates; read another user's deliveries; mute the risk channel; point a webhook at the Tailscale control plane or a metadata endpoint; flood the evaluator; forge an ack.
- Risk rating (likelihood × impact) with an owner and a target ticket per Critical/High finding; residual risk recorded in `docs/plan/32-risk-register.md` under R11.
- Data-classification table: alert definitions Internal; `webhook_url_enc`/`webhook_secret_enc` SECRET; `alert_deliveries.context` Internal but may quote market state and position values, so it is scoped to the owning user.
- Output: `docs/security/threat-models/e40-alerts.md`, reviewed with the Architect and the epic owner.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
- **Abuse-case suite** (`tests/security/alerts/`), each case from the threat model, run as a **required check**:
  1. *Action smuggling* — a corpus of payloads placing action nodes at every position in the IR tree (top level, inside `variables`, inside a nested condition, via an operand referencing an action, via an unknown node kind); every one must 422 with no OMS interaction. Plus a property test (hypothesis) over generated IR trees asserting no tree containing an action node compiles, and the enumeration test asserting every node kind in E35's registry is either allow-listed or rejected.
  2. *Template exfiltration* — placeholders naming SECRET columns, traversal-style placeholders, and placeholders resolving to another user's context; all must 422.
  3. *Cross-user access* — the full matrix: user A attempts GET/PUT/DELETE/enable on B's alert, ack on B's delivery, list with B's `alert_id`, subscribe to WS `alerts` expecting B's deliveries; every combination must fail with no state change and an audit row.
  4. *Risk-channel muting* — direct API attempts to mute an override-listed category must be rejected and audited as `notifications.risk_channel_muted`.
  5. *Delivery forgery* — a client attempting to create or ack a delivery it does not own, or to inject a delivery over the WS connection.
  6. *SSRF corpus* (used by E40-S03 in R5, written now so the egress path is built against it): loopback in decimal/octal/IPv6-mapped forms, link-local `169.254.169.254`, RFC1918 outside the Tailscale CIDR, userinfo-in-URL tricks, redirect-to-blocked, DNS-rebinding with a mutating resolver.
  7. *Resource exhaustion* — exceeding the per-user alert cap, `ack-all` with a very large unacked set, evaluation-queue flooding; each must degrade with a counted metric rather than a stall.
- **Scope assertions**: an automated matrix over every `/alerts*` and `/notifications` route × every role (owner / manager / viewer) asserting the expected allow/deny, no state change on deny, and an audit row — the alert slice of the R3 exit criterion "an automated matrix test exercises every route × every role".
- **SAST rules**: Semgrep rules banning (a) `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in alert/notification components, (b) constructing an outbound HTTP request in the alerts package outside the hardened egress client, (c) selecting `webhook_url_enc`/`webhook_secret_enc` outside the credential-broker path, (d) deny-list-style checks on IR node kinds (the fail-open pattern).
- **DAST**: an OWASP ZAP profile covering the alert configuration endpoints, wired into the nightly security job.
- **Secrets scanning** over alert fixtures and test artifacts.
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
- **Code review** of the security-relevant paths with the threat model open: `cv/alerts/compiler.py` (the allow-list and its fail-closed property), `cv/alerts/evaluator.py` (per-user caps, queue bounds, the firing transaction), `cv/alerts/dispatcher.py` (per-channel isolation, ack ownership resolution, `ack-all` bounding), the `/notifications` union (per-source scoping), the WS `alerts` topic authorisation, the SECRET-column read allow-list in the repository, and the frontend text-rendering paths.
- **Threat-model re-validation**: confirm the E40-X01 data-flow diagram matches what shipped; update it where it does not; re-rate any threat whose likelihood or impact changed during implementation.
- **Findings triage**: every Critical/High closed, or accepted-risk with a written rationale and **Owner sign-off**; Medium/Low triaged with target tickets (E43 hardening where appropriate).
- **Manual abuse-case pass** beyond the automated suite: attempt privilege escalation from an alert, attempt to read another user's notification history through the union endpoint, attempt to silence a risk notification through the preference API, attempt to forge an ack, and attempt to construct an alert whose message template exfiltrates context from another scope.
- **Verification of the descoped webhook posture**: confirm `alerts.webhook_enabled` is off in every environment, that no code path writes `webhook_url` in R3, and that the SSRF corpus is in place for the R5 implementation; record this explicitly so R4/R5 inherit an accurate picture.
- **Supply chain**: SCA (pip-audit/npm audit) clean or triaged for the dependencies E40 introduced; secrets scan clean.
- Sign-off comment on E40 recording the review scope, findings, dispositions and residual risk; feed the residuals into the E43 pen-test scope.

## Out of scope
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
Implementing controls (E40-T02/T03/T04, E40-X01) and the final review (E40-X01). Pen-testing (E43).
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
The final review and sign-off (E40-X01). Implementing the webhook adapter itself (E40-S03). Pen-testing (E43).
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
Building new controls (E40-X01). Pen-testing itself (E43). Live enablement gating (E44).

## Acceptance criteria
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
```gherkin
Scenario: Every element and flow is analysed
  When the model is reviewed against the data-flow diagram
  Then each element and each flow has a STRIDE row, or an explicit "not applicable" with a reason
Scenario: The elevation path is treated as the primary threat
  Then the "an alert can act" threat is rated and traced to a named, testable control in E40-T02, not merely to a design intention
Scenario: Abuse cases are executable (edge)
  Then each abuse case is written concretely enough that E40-X01 can automate it without further interpretation
Scenario: An unmitigated High is escalated (failure)
  Given a High finding with no control landing in R3
  Then it is recorded as accepted risk with Owner sign-off, or the epic scope changes; it is not left silently open
```
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
```gherkin
Scenario: The core invariant is proven, not asserted
  When the action-smuggling corpus, the property test and the node-kind enumeration test run
  Then every payload is rejected, no generated tree containing an action compiles, and every node kind in E35's registry is accounted for
Scenario: A future E35 node kind cannot silently widen the surface (edge)
  Given a new node kind is added to E35's registry without updating the alert allow-list
  Then the enumeration test fails in CI, blocking the merge
Scenario: The role matrix is exhaustive
  Then every alert route is exercised against every role, and each denied combination shows 403 or 404, no state change, and an audit row
Scenario: SSRF payloads are refused before connecting (failure)
  Given each entry of the SSRF corpus
  Then the egress policy refuses before any socket is opened, and the refusal increments cv_alert_webhook_blocked_total
Scenario: A SAST rule catches a reintroduced pattern (failure)
  Given a commit adding raw HTML rendering to a notification component
  Then the Semgrep rule fails the build naming the file and line
```
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
```gherkin
Scenario: The shipped system matches the modelled system
  When the data-flow diagram is walked against the merged code
  Then every element and flow is accounted for, and any divergence is corrected in the model
Scenario: The core invariant holds under manual attack
  Given a determined manual attempt to make an alert place, amend or cancel an order by any path
  Then every attempt fails, is logged, and is visible in the audit trail
Scenario: Every Critical and High is dispositioned (failure)
  Given an open Critical or High finding
  Then it is fixed before sign-off, or recorded as accepted risk with a written rationale and Owner sign-off; sign-off is not given otherwise
Scenario: The webhook posture is verifiable (edge)
  When the deployed configuration is inspected in every environment
  Then alerts.webhook_enabled is off, no alert row carries a webhook URL, and the finding is recorded for the R4/R5 gate
Scenario: Residual risk is carried forward (edge)
  Then each residual is recorded in the risk register under R11 and added to the E43 pen-test scope, not closed silently
```

## Technical notes / design
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
Model against the **as-designed** system from `docs/plan/20-architecture.md` and the E40 tickets, and re-validate the diagram against the implementation during E40-X01 — a threat model that describes a system nobody built is worse than none.

Pay specific attention to the future-proofing of the elevation control: E35 will add node kinds over time, so the model must require an allow-list (fail-closed) rather than a deny-list, and require a test that enumerates E35's registry.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
The property test is the load-bearing part of case 1: an enumerated corpus proves the cases someone imagined, while the property test plus the registry-enumeration test covers the ones they did not. Both must run as required checks, not nightly.

The role matrix reuses the shared RBAC test harness from E09/E29 rather than a bespoke one, so a permission-model change is caught everywhere at once.

The SSRF corpus is written now even though E40-S03 is R5, because writing the egress path against an existing corpus produces a materially safer implementation than retrofitting tests to it.
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
Review against the merged `main`, not a branch, so the review covers the integrated system including any interaction between E40 and E35/E39 that only appears after merge.

Pay particular attention to interaction risks: an alert on an E39 risk metric, a notification preference that could suppress an E39 lockout signal, and the `/notifications` union pulling `order_events` the caller may not read.

## Test plan
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
N/A — analysis. Verification is that every Critical/High finding maps to a test in E40-X01 or E40-Q01.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
The suite is the deliverable. Validate by mutation: weaken the compiler's allow-list to a deny-list and confirm the property test fails; remove the `scope: self` dependency and confirm the role matrix fails; disable the redirect ban and confirm the SSRF corpus fails.
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
Manual review plus the execution of the E40-X01 suite on the release candidate; any manual finding that can be automated gets a test filed before sign-off.

## Security notes
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
The document itself describes attack paths and is classified Internal; store in the repo (private) and do not quote it in public issue text.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
This ticket implements the controls for E40-X01's Critical/High findings. Any finding without a test here must be explicitly listed in E40-X01 as accepted risk with Owner sign-off. Test payloads are adversarial by design and must never run against live.
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
This ticket *is* the security verification for the epic. Its output is the sign-off comment plus the residual-risk entries; both are inputs to the R3 PRR and the R4 pen-test scoping.

## Accessibility notes
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
Include the "assistive technology reads redacted content" threat explicitly — it is routinely missed and is a real information-disclosure path.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
Includes an assertion that no accessible name, description or live-region announcement in the alert surfaces contains a SECRET-classified value — the automated half of the E40-Q02 manual check.
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
Confirms the E40-Q02 finding that no assistive-technology surface exposes SECRET-classified content.

## Performance notes
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
Denial-of-service findings must state numeric limits (alerts per user, evaluation queue depth, ack-all batch size) so the implementing tickets have a target rather than an adjective.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
The exhaustion cases assert graceful degradation with counted metrics, and must themselves be bounded so the security suite does not become the slowest job in CI (target ≤6 min).
### Part C — Security review and sign-off of the shipped system
Verifies the DoS controls are actually configured, not merely implemented: per-user alert cap, evaluation queue bound, `ack-all` batch cap, and their alerting thresholds.

## Observability
### Part A — STRIDE threat model for the alert and notification surface
Specify the security-relevant telemetry E40 must emit: `cv_alert_compile_rejected_total{reason="action_node"}` (any non-zero value is an attempted invariant breach), `cv_alert_webhook_blocked_total{reason}`, and the `notifications.risk_channel_muted` audit event.
### Part B — Abuse-case suite, scope assertions and SAST/DAST rules
Verifies that `cv_alert_compile_rejected_total{reason="action_node"}`, `cv_alert_webhook_blocked_total{reason}` and the audit events are emitted on every rejection — a silent rejection is a monitoring gap.

title: Design QA of the built journal screens against the hi-fi
body:
## Context
Design QA closes the loop: the built SCR-093..096 are compared frame-by-frame against the signed-off hi-fi and handoff package, with every deviation either fixed or explicitly accepted by the CDO. Without this pass, the sign-off checklists in `docs/plan/14-screens-catalogue.md` are aspirational rather than verified.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Side-by-side review of each built screen against its hi-fi in both themes, at the default density, at 200% zoom and at the minimum supported window size.
- Verification that **tokens** are used rather than hard-coded values (spot-check computed styles against `docs/plan/16-design-system-brief.md` token names).
- Verification of all declared states by driving the app into them: empty, loading, partial ("chart context unavailable"), reconciling, insufficient sample, "context not recorded", tag-merge confirmation.
- Verification of the copy deck: every string in the build matches the approved copy exactly.
- Verification of motion incl. the `prefers-reduced-motion` variants.
- A defect list filed as Bug tickets with severity, each linked to this ticket; blockers must be fixed before the E41-Q03 sign-off.

## Out of scope
- Functional correctness of statistics (E41-Q01/Q02); accessibility conformance testing (E41-Q03) - though obvious a11y regressions found here are filed.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every state inspected
  When design QA runs
  Then each state declared for SCR-093, SCR-094, SCR-095 and SCR-096 has been driven in the real build and evidenced with a screenshot

Scenario: Deviations resolved
  Given a visual deviation from the signed-off hi-fi is found
  Then it is filed as a Bug with severity and is either fixed or recorded as an accepted deviation with a CDO comment before this ticket closes

Scenario: Tokens not hexes
  When computed styles are sampled on 10 representative elements per screen
  Then each resolves to a design-system token value and no ad hoc colour or spacing is present
```

## Technical notes / design
States that are awkward to reach are driven with seeded fixtures: `journal_fixture_empty`, `journal_fixture_12_trades` (low sample), `journal_fixture_10k` (density), `journal_fixture_pruned_context`, `journal_fixture_reconciling` - the same fixtures E41-Q01 defines, reused rather than duplicated.

## Test plan
Manual structured pass with a checklist derived from the four sign-off checklists; screenshots attached per state; Storybook visual snapshots for CMP-166..169 reviewed alongside.

## Security notes
The pass is run as each of Owner, Manager and Viewer to confirm the RBAC-dependent copy and scoping variants render as designed (feeds E41-X02 evidence).

## Accessibility notes
Reduced-motion variants and visible focus rings are checked here; deeper conformance testing is E41-Q03.

## Performance notes
The 10k-trade fixture pass doubles as a subjective check that scrolling and filtering feel within the budgets E41-Q02 measures numerically.

## Observability
N/A.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] All four screens reviewed in both themes, at 200% zoom and minimum window size.
- [ ] Every declared state evidenced with a screenshot.
- [ ] Defects filed; blockers closed; accepted deviations recorded with CDO comments.
- [ ] Storybook visual snapshots for CMP-166, CMP-167, CMP-168, CMP-169 reviewed and approved.
